title: Chicago: the Green Mill Gardens audition, Isham Jones and Vic Berton
summary: He recounts sitting in at the Chicago club, getting the job, Isham Jones's interest and drummer Vic Berton; the long answer also covers his finances and being named a jazz model.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: No, he... No, the book didn't... This... Durrell Black. Wasn't it Durrell Black? No, it was with Al Rose. I know. They sent me a testimonial, and I'm a jazzy model, and my daughter has his frame. I guess they sent out a million of them, because Dr. Block says, I'm waiting until you see you come out. You never came out. I said, I don't leave the house at night, Dr. Block. I said, I have a sick wife, because you know you're treating her, you know. Well, this... My daughter's so proud of it, she had it framed in it. She gives lots of court parties, and has lots of friendships. It's a topic of discussion, that I am a jazzy model. Why did they make me a jazzy model when I was in the business? I'm great now. Everybody knows the great John McIndra. But when I was in the business, I had to hustle like the rest of them. You mean, huh? Everybody... Every musician has his ups and downs. I didn't have any downs. I always prepared for the rainy day, because I... I never gambled. And I bought property. When the pressure came, I was land poor. But that's why I can live here. Don't worry what I'm going to eat. Ask for no favors. And I didn't buy any clothes all the while. My wife was sick. I bought two complete suits, and a board coat, and trousers, and that yesterday. Because my daughter said, Daddy, you don't have to dress that way. I don't care how... I have fallen away, I went down. But I look clean. I'm always clean. And my band was always impeccable. It took me a lot to let them wear soft shirts with a tuxedo. But I found out how good it was. When I went to work at the Greenville Garden, I'm the only man in the band with a stiff shirt. And I had a weak car. Charlie McNeil, the world's greatest band choice at that time, he was the first man to write the chord systems. You know, chord walking, you go... Yes, I played with him. In fact, he was a piano repair man for all the ballad and the cat's theaters, and the trombone player was the mechanic. He'd go there and condemn the pianos and the trombone player would repair them. He had a beautiful racket. I'm telling you right now. He whispers in my ear one night, Johnny, don't answer me. I said, what? Isham Jones wants to see you. Remember Isham Jones? No. He was playing at the Rainbow Gardens down the street. I'm playing at the Greenville. Wood gets around, there's a guy at the Greenville, he can play the trumpet. Isham Jones wants to get a hold of me. But I'm important. The union had known it, they had thrown me out bodily. I was brought... The way I made my entrance into the Greenville Gardens, I went there one night, put my trumpet in the bar, sat at the table and listened to the band. I walked up to Johnson. He knows all about it. He's in coach with the boss. I said, I see you don't have a trumpet. You know, you quit. I said, I'm a trumpet player. I said, where are you from? I said, New Orleans, he knows all about it. New Orleans. When you say New Orleans, it's made. It's made. And you better be hot. I said, may I sit in? He said, sure. Get your horn. Where's your horn? I said, the horn is on the bar. So I get the horn, I take it out, I sit down. He said, where do you want to play? I said, anything. Well, I went for the musicians. He said, anything. Well, you know what to pick out. Pick out a couple of standards. You know Dixieland standards. Not having any trumpet. I saw like ten trumpets. And I played well. I had the job in the pot. Because the boss had wanted me his car and his chauffeur to find me an apartment. He used to give me a beer at the cost. And the luckiest thing after going all over Chicago, and I'm sitting in the back of his car, they had half a top. Oh, he had plenty of money. And his chauffeur, my wife, they want to take children. I don't know, they didn't want children. Around the corner from where I'm waiting, I get in the most beautiful apartment, and the man who wanted it was in all this. This is one of the big theaters. And he had a little girl. And he went right fire with my little girl. But she did say, I want to see your daughter. And when I saw her daughter, that was a wildcat. But my daughter was with behavior. Everything worked that way. Their daughter ate in my house, in my apartment all the time. So Issa Jones wants to see me. Then Paul Beesey. You ever hear of Paul Beesey? I've heard the name, but I don't remember if I ever had any hearing. He was a stout man. They operated on him. He took 60 pounds off his stomach and he died. Like that. When he sat at the table for two, he needed to the table for two. The guys in the band said to me, look who's listening to you. I said, you listen to me? He's listening to you. Maurice Sherman, after his leader at the Sher... Marlin, this leader in the Sherman house. He said, I think his name was Sherman. He was a Marlinist. We had a conglomerate mess. We didn't have any band. We had one incident of each. Piano, violin, tenor saxophone, trumpet, trombone, and drums. And the drummer was Victor Burton who wrote the Sob and Blues. You know the Sob and Blues? Oh yeah.
I know him from his records with Nichols and the Wolverines.
Well, his name is Vic Cohen, if you want to know his name.
I know his little brother. I didn't know that was his name.
